quotes.briefing_quote: Planners highlighted that the historic Middletown District, centered at Main and Church Streets, represents an excellent example of 'turnpike town' development, which was later influenced by the 1896 electric trolley that connected the region to wider parts of the county.

To encourage commercial and mixed-use investment in timeless older buildings, the Town of Middletown offers Downtown Revitalization Zone incentives—including water and sewer fee reductions and parking waivers—for developers who invest at least $250,000 and preserve the historic front facades.

The plan notes that outlying developments, including West Middletown Estates and Picnic Woods Estates, represent a highly desirable area for residential development, though this trend increasingly conflicts with existing agricultural operations in the surrounding valley.
The county is moving forward with constructing a new 15,250 square-foot branch library on land deeded adjacent to East Green Street, expanding critical civic programming and resources.

Due to severe local groundwater limitations during drought conditions, Middletown's growth policies dictate that developers seeking annexation must find and secure their own water rights and provide 250 gallons of allocable water per unit prior to annexation approval.

geographic_addresses: 31 West Main Street, Middletown, MD
Alternate US 40 & MD 17, Middletown, MD

quotes.briefing_quote: The ambitious $4-million rehabilitation of the historic Memorial Hall at 4 East Main Street, which stood empty for nearly 50 years, successfully created 15 new luxury apartments and two commercial spaces.

A private developer renovated the historic Valley Register Building at 123 West Main Street into five small apartments and a ground-floor commercial space, which was fully leased within a month of opening.

To encourage downtown investment, the Town established the Middletown Revitalization Zone Incentive Package, which enables eligible projects to move quickly through the planning process and provides lower fees for Main Street District commercial renovations exceeding $250,000.

Middletown faces a lack of affordable housing and high housing costs, prompting goals to audit municipal ordinances and examine code changes that could support a wider variety of housing types for citizens of all incomes and ages.

Middletown is mandated by the Maryland Department of the Environment to complete a $40 million wastewater treatment plant renovation by 2026, representing a massive infrastructure commitment for the town.

While Middletown enjoys an agricultural-rich surrounding valley, there is constant pressure for growth in surrounding farm areas, requiring careful management to preserve the town's small-town charm and prevent excessive sprawl.

While public parking in Middletown is functional, local planners note a persistent public perception of insufficient parking, highlighting a need to improve signage and greening in downtown lots to make walking a few hundred feet more inviting.

quotes.briefing_quote: Town staff highlighted that while Sustainable Myersville remains a relatively homogeneous and economically affluent community, younger families and individuals are moving in to replace older residents, which has begun lowering the median age even as regional housing costs remain exceptionally high.

The Sustainable Communities Workgroup reported a challenging climate for commercial retention, noting that since 2020, a local diner, beauty salon, and gunsmith have closed their doors without attracting new businesses due to a lack of commercial tax incentives and the reinstatement of the business personal property tax.

Planners successfully amended the municipal zoning code to allow for higher density development and accessory dwelling units, targeting greater housing stock diversity and affordability in an otherwise exclusive market.

Municipal officials noted that local development projects face headwinds, as residents have historically resisted government policies targeting specific developments, with proposed infill projects routinely drawing scrutiny from the community at-large.

The Action Plan identifies a critical gap in regional connectivity, explaining that the primary barrier to accessing public transportation is safely crossing Interstate 70 and its high-speed ramps to reach the commuter bus lot on Ventrie Court.

quotes.briefing_quote: The historic heart of Myersville is defined by the Myersville Survey District, a linear 35-acre corridor along Main Street containing over 100 structures built between 1830 and 1939. This area serves as a good example of a small town that grew slowly around agricultural services before experiencing a moderate development boom driven by the electric railway.

While Myersville's growth and more sophisticated architectural styles were heavily accelerated by the introduction of the electric trolley line in 1898, neighboring Wolfsville represents how the community might have developed had it remained a small, traditional crossroads settlement without early rail transit influences.

In 2019, Frederick County completed a new 7,500 square-foot branch library on Harp Place. Erected on the site of the former school, this facility serves as an educational and cultural hub, complete with a dedicated 'Trolley Room' featuring a restored historic trolley car that celebrates the town's electric railway heritage.

Because water resource availability is the primary constraint on local growth, large-scale density increases are difficult. However, local planners suggest that permitting accessory dwelling units could provide critical affordable housing options and allow seniors to age in place without placing excessive strain on municipal water systems.

During the annexation of the Quail Run subdivision, the town successfully leveraged an annexation agreement to require the developer to include 30 townhouse units alongside single-family homes, demonstrating a practical regulatory mechanism for diversifying housing types in new developments.

quotes.briefing_quote: The Town of New Market has seen dramatic demographic shifts, with the population increasing by approximately 130% over a nine-year period to 1,551 residents, accompanied by a decrease in median age to 34.2 years and an increase in average household size.

Historically a walkable corridor community centered on the Old National Road, New Market's Main Street became a heavily traveled cut-through corridor following the construction of Interstate 70, which has created ongoing pedestrian-vehicular conflicts and altered the friendly image of the historic core.

The town is moving forward with the North Alley Improvements and Stormwater Infrastructure project, a $1.246 million effort in partnership with the state to upgrade stormwater facilities, rebuild road beds, and improve pedestrian and vehicular safety.

Local planning efforts for the proposed Calumet subdivision have faced persistent delays because a sewer and water allocation agreement could not be finalized between the county and the town, illustrating the complexity of political and infrastructure alignment in growth areas.

Repurposing the vacant historic Old Town Hall at 39 West Main Street has been hindered by prohibitive commercial water and sewer tap fees, ADA compliance hurdles, and structural integrity concerns that challenge the economic feasibility of commercial tenants.

Through the Façade Improvement Program administered by the New Market Civic Partnership, the town distributed multiple rounds of matching grants to property owners, successfully leveraging private investment to visually upgrade and stabilize historic properties along Main Street.

quotes.briefing_quote: According to historical records, Highland Beach was founded in 1893 as the first summer resort area for prominent African Americans, envisioned by Major Charles Douglass and his wife Laura after they were turned away from a resort in neighboring Bay Ridge due to their race.

Town planners note that Highland Beach remains an exclusively residential enclave of both seasonal and year-round households that explicitly choose not to permit commercial establishments, preserving a legacy where many of the 77 homes are still owned by descendants of the original settlers.

Planning documents highlight that land use has evolved rapidly, with twenty-one new homes constructed on previously vacant lots since 1990, alongside the replacement and extensive renovation of original historic cottages.

To protect the town's small-town character, residents and officials recommend maintaining and enforcing the codified minimum lot area standard of 15,000 square feet and the existing two-lot minimum for new home construction.

As a major community preservation success, the historic Twin Oaks summer cottage built in 1895 for Frederick Douglass was successfully restored and converted into the Frederick Douglass Museum and Cultural Center, serving as a national historic asset.

quotes.briefing_quote: By the late 19th century, Walkersville had transformed from a simple agricultural supply point into a thriving village. In 1887, a local observer described it as having "more building enterprise than any other village in the county" alongside some of the region's finest historic residences.

The Town's core vision is centered on maintaining its small-town character by strictly limiting municipal growth and preserving the agricultural buffer that physically separates the community from surrounding urbanizing jurisdictions.
The Old Town area of Walkersville presents a compact, pedestrian-scaled environment defined by a historic grid street pattern and an organic mix of single-, two-, and multi-family housing styles.

Even where local zoning might permit accessory dwelling units (ADUs), planners caution that construction can be cost-prohibitive for property owners due to substantial municipal water and sewer tap fees, as well as county-wide impact fees.

To protect the gateway into the historic core, planners suggest rezoning properties along East Frederick Street to B-1 to ensure future redevelopments maintain a pedestrian-friendly scale and prevent the intrusion of automobile-oriented uses like gas stations.

The planned Frederick and Pennsylvania Line Railroad Trail will construct a ten-foot-wide paved multi-use pathway within the historic rail right-of-way, eventually connecting Walkersville's Heritage Farm Park directly to the City of Frederick's trail network.

quotes.briefing_quote: One of the notable strengths of the Golden Mile lies in its accessibility, with almost 25,000 individuals residing within a convenient walk or drive of the commercial corridor. Currently, many new residential projects — Summers Farm, West Park Village, Waverly View, Belle Aire Farm, Westridge, and Grove Hill — are underway. Collectively, these projects will introduce around 2,000 new units to the corridor.

Planning staff highlighted successful adaptive reuse projects, notably including the Visitation Academy, Union Knitting Mills, and Ox Fiber Apartments, which successfully preserve historic structures and drive economic revitalization.

To encourage higher density and affordable housing, the City enacted a text amendment to Section 420 of the Land Management Code for the Carroll Creek Overlay District, which eliminated the restriction on density to make the maximum density for Downtown Business properties the same inside the overlay as it is outside, while increasing density further when structured parking is built.
The East Frederick Region is undergoing significant expansion, highlighted by the Renn Farm development, which introduces 1,000 new units and 30 acres of both passive and active parkland.

City planning efforts are focused on crafting a Form-Based Code for the East Street Corridor, which will place the emphasis on design rather than use to enhance the attributes unique to the corridor, promote greater housing choices, and encourage equitable development.

quotes.briefing_quote: According to demographic records, the Town of Lonaconing has seen a modest population growth of 0.313% between 2019 and 2020, alongside a 12.5% increase in median household income to $47,824. The town remains highly affordable with a median property value of $72,600 and a 58.5% homeownership rate.

The community retains a deep historical connection to its roots as a 'company town' owned by the Georges Creek Coal and Iron Company. Preserving heritage assets, such as the 19th-century Kelly's Tavern and the historic Iron Furnace, remains central to the town's character and preservation efforts.

The town completed construction on the Pekin-Moscow water line in the fall of 2022. This critical infrastructure project resolved a massive water loss issue where leaks caused the loss of 400,000 gallons of water per day, which had previously run the system dry and left residents without water.

A significant hurdle for new residential development in Lonaconing is the complete lack of buildable land within municipal boundaries, meaning any future residential growth must rely on the creative reuse or redevelopment of existing lots.

The development of a new Dollar General store and the construction of the new Town Hall both serve as successful case studies of demolishing blighted, vacant houses to execute infill development within the town's core.

quotes.briefing_quote: Plan data indicates that the population and population density have both decreased in Frostburg between 2010 and 2021, marking a 22% overall decrease that represents a divergence from previous decades where student population growth drove steady increases.

Planning staff observed that one of the city’s biggest obstacles in development is a lack of buildable land due to the largely built-out nature of the municipality, combined with the difficult economics of assembling multiple uniquely-shaped lots for redevelopment in Allegany County.

In a major institutional development, Frostburg State University received the old City Hall building as a donation and will invest $6 million to rehabilitate and convert the structure into a new regional science and educational center.

To better accommodate tourism and flexible property usage, the City recently updated its Zoning Ordinance to facilitate short-term vacation rentals, eliminating obstacles for property owners in high-density areas near the downtown and university campus.

Addressing housing challenges, the plan notes that vacant residential properties increased to 17.49% of all housing units in 2020, up from 14.88% in 2015, a trend linked to overall population loss and the city's aging housing stock.

quotes.briefing_quote: Demographic trends indicate that the total population within the Aberdeen Sustainable Community area grew by 3% to 10,724 residents between 2015 and 2019, while the median household income rose by 28% and the unemployment rate fell by 41%.

To leverage transit assets, the city secured a $700,000 Transportation Alternative Program grant to improve pedestrian and bicycle connectivity around the Aberdeen MARC and Amtrak Train Station, detailing plans for new public sidewalks, lighting, landscaping, and ADA compliance upgrades.

Local planning officials identified that Aberdeen's housing stock faces challenges because the city lacks a municipal property maintenance code and a rental registration program, which can hinder the renovation of older housing and lead to local livability violations.

To attract investment to the commercial core, the city amended its zoning code to permit breweries, distilleries, and wineries within several business and industrial zones, while also waiving parking requirements in the Transit Oriented Development district.

Demonstrating commercial and residential rehabilitation, a private investor successfully purchased and renovated the Parke Street Apartments through Opportunity Zone incentives, while public grants facilitated the demolition of five blighted properties along North Philadelphia Boulevard, Franklin Street, and East Bel Air Avenue.

Heavy commercial activity has created significant traffic congestion on MD-7 and MD-715 due to tractor trailers navigating between major regional distribution facilities in the Aberdeen area and the Perryman Peninsula.

quotes.briefing_quote: The downtown area features a diverse mix of retail, dining, and service options, dominated by a strong professional office presence. This unique layout creates a vibrant daytime population that supports local businesses, though many historic properties lack dedicated on-site parking and sit close to the street, adding to the district's walkable, eclectic charm.

Bel Air has served as a courthouse town for over two centuries, tracing its roots back to 1782 when it became the county seat under the name 'Scott's Old Fields.' The historic core originated on and near Main Street, preserving a legacy that continues to define the town's architectural and cultural identity today.

University of Maryland Upper Chesapeake Health is expanding its medical campus in Bel Air by adding three floors to the Kaufman Cancer Center. This 50,000-square-foot expansion will introduce seventy-two additional patient beds and state-of-the-art treatment spaces by 2023, solidifying the facility as a regional healthcare hub.

Planning analyses indicate that market-rate apartments and condominiums are exceptionally well-suited for the area due to its walkable design and close proximity to downtown amenities. Developing high-end residential units can help satisfy strong housing demand from both empty-nesters and incoming young professionals.

Recent residential developments demonstrate the viability of diverse housing forms, including the Townes at Bynum Run and the Overlook at Gateway Condominiums. Notably, the Bel Air Academy redevelopment on East Gordon Street stands out as a successful adaptive reuse model, converting a historic schoolhouse into modern residential units.

Balancing new, high-density development with historic housing stock remains a key local challenge driven by resident desires to preserve a small-town feel. Planners suggest that introducing visually compatible, moderately dense housing in established neighborhoods can successfully expand the housing supply without eroding community character.

The Town successfully established the Armory Marketplace Incubator Program to support new and emerging businesses. The highly competitive program offers entrepreneurs a below-market lease rate for a maximum of three years, allowing them to build financial assets before relocating to permanent commercial space in Bel Air.

To address the lack of age-appropriate and affordable housing, the plan suggests targeting underutilized downtown properties. Redeveloping underutilized parking lots into productive commercial or residential mixed-use developments can create viable opportunities for empty-nesters and young professionals.

To address commercial blight and create a walkable destination, the Town developed a Green Concept Plan for Burns Alley. The project will convert approximately one acre of impervious land into a walkable destination with access to restaurants, new commercial spaces, and an increased tree canopy.

quotes.briefing_quote: The Town of Eagle Harbor, located along the Patuxent River waterfront, was founded in 1929 as an African American resort town that catered specifically to the middle-class Black population of nearby Washington, D.C. Over the decades, as racial segregation ended and black residents gained access to integrated beaches, the seasonal resort aspect faded and the permanent population declined.

With the median age of Eagle Harbor rising to 62.7 years, the aging population presents a significant challenge for local accessibility and medical care access. It has become imperative for the town's viability to attract new and possibly younger residents to the community, especially as inherited properties face maintenance neglect.

Eagle Harbor recently received a congressional designation as a National Heritage Area as part of the Southern Maryland National Heritage Area. This designation provides local access to regional grant funding of up to $10 million over 10 years to support historic and cultural preservation efforts.

New residential construction in Eagle Harbor has been heavily restricted by a local lot consolidation requirement demanding six or more adjoining lots to bring public water and sewer infrastructure, which inhibits housing development by smaller builders.

Environmental regulations, though strongly supported by the community, often conflict with development goals because a portion of the town lies in a FEMA flood zone. Future construction must be concentrated outside of wetlands and floodplains while navigating strict Chesapeake Bay Critical Area regulations.

The Eagle Harbor Stream Restoration and Community Resiliency Project is an ongoing effort to construct a climate-resilient, nature-based stream restoration along Coleman Creek and a living shoreline along the Patuxent River to mitigate runoff and upland flooding.

quotes.briefing_quote: The Town of Chesapeake Beach is executing a deliberate strategy to limit expansion, proposing to reduce zoned development capacity by 53 percent from 489 units to just 230 over the next twenty years. Growth will be heavily restricted to completing currently approved subdivision projects and limited infill on vacant parcels, representing an average annual growth rate of just 0.5 percent.

Developers scoping new construction in Chesapeake Beach should prepare for strict aesthetic scrutiny, as planning officials reject formulaic building design and franchise architecture that conflicts with the town's maritime character. Future developments will be expected to harmonize with the existing cottage scale, massing, and historic context, with new regulations slated to cap building heights at 35 feet and eliminate density bonuses.

Tracing its origins to a late-19th-century grand resort design, Chesapeake Beach is defined by its original cottage neighborhoods built on small lots. The plan aims to preserve these enduring landmarks by recommending voluntary restoration, rehabilitation grants, loans, and historic tax credits, particularly to protect the cottage character along the approach to Bayside Road.

Addressing climate vulnerabilities, the updated plan recommends prohibiting further development or residential uses in areas expected to be submerged by a projected 2.1-foot sea level rise by 2050. These low-lying and high-risk zones, concentrated around Fishing Creek and parts of Bayside Road, will be downzoned to Resource Conservation to prevent exposing new properties to unacceptably high flood risks.

Chesapeake Beach and neighboring North Beach form the interconnected 'twin beaches' coastal community. quotes.briefing_quote: Sharpsburg's physical footprint is highly constrained, as the town is bounded on all sides by National Parks, agricultural lands, and strict preservation easements that prevent outward expansion and greenfield development.

To address central parking shortages, the town demolished the obsolete American Legion building to create a designated tourist and resident parking lot featuring a prominent historical mural by a local artist.

With approximately 342 mostly single-family homes, the local market remains relatively affordable, though there is an increasing need to support aging-in-place home renovations for the town's substantial senior population.

The municipal zoning framework features a dedicated town center district with regulations designed to limit chain retailers and big-box development to preserve the neighborhood's residential character and historic small-town charm.
In a major effort to secure its historical fabric, the town has purchased a one-acre parcel to develop a new interpretive pocket park and plaza, while pursuing acquisition of the historic Big Spring.

quotes.briefing_quote: Baltimore City's neighborhoods of Broening Manor, Graceland Park, Medford, and O'Donnell Heights were historically developed around industry as workforce housing in response to World War II, housing workers from major nearby employers like Bethlehem Steel and Martin Aircraft.

In 1942, O'Donnell Heights was built as a temporary shelter for wartime steel and aircraft workers before eventually being converted to public housing, followed by decades of disinvestment and population loss.

The residential units for future phases of Key's Pointe should be designed to reflect the vernacular architectural character found in the surrounding community, including porches with free-standing and attached columns, proper trim, and brick surfaces rather than looking overly institutional.

The city's first two net-zero energy K-8 schools—Graceland Park Elementary/Middle School and Holabird Academy—were constructed within three blocks of each other, providing state-of-the-art shared collaborative learning spaces and community hubs.

The joint development team of The Michaels Development Company and Greater Baltimore AHC led the redevelopment of O'Donnell Heights into Key's Pointe, completing Phase 1A in 2014 with 76 units and Phase 1B in 2018 with 68 units as a precedent for modern mixed-income housing.

quotes.briefing_quote: Constructed as a tight-knit rowhouse community beginning in the 1890s, Easterwood soon became known for its small busy shops, churches, and businesses run by local residents. The neighborhood was transformed in the mid-1940s to mid-1950s by rapid desegregation, shifting from a wholly Jewish community to virtually all African-American within a single decade.

While much of West Baltimore is designated as Opportunity Zones, census tracts defining Easterwood and Coppin Heights are notably omitted. Community advocates highlight that the neighborhood is frequently overlooked for public investments and social services, which have historically been concentrated in adjacent Sandtown.

To address vacant mid-block lots, the community advocates for infilling these neglected spaces with small, handicap-accessible bungalows. This single-family infill strategy aims to diversify housing options, provide affordable opportunities for legacy residents to age in place, and eliminate hotspots for illegal dumping.

Easterwood's housing market displays a distinct east-west divide, where well-maintained blocks with high homeowner occupancy lie near Easterwood Park and Matthew Henson Elementary, while housing conditions deteriorate toward the eastern quadrant near Monroe Street with a high concentration of vacant properties.

quotes.briefing_quote: Established in the 1940s as a planned suburb for Black WWII veterans, Cherry Hill remains a predominantly African-American community with deep-rooted community pride, despite historic physical isolation and a high concentration of public housing.

To meet modern family standards, housing developers should move away from historic 750-to-900 square foot floor plans and instead provide 3-to-4 bedroom units with multiple bathrooms and features built around CPTED principles.

quotes.briefing_quote: Friendsville maintains a small-town atmosphere where visitors can experience the charm of a close-knit community with local shops and friendly residents, all while being surrounded by picturesque mountain landscapes and the Youghiogheny River.

Dating back to the late 1700s when it was established as a trading post for fur trappers and traders, Friendsville's rich historical heritage has left a legacy of historic buildings and sites that shape its modern built environment.

The community is advancing plans for the construction of a brand-new Friendsville Library building, designed by architects Murphy and Dittenhafer and supported by a grant from the Maryland State Library on land donated by the Town.

As the local population continues to age, planners note a critical shortage of housing options tailored to seniors, prompting the town to actively seek out developers who can deliver accessible, sustainable options that allow residents to age in place.

To facilitate revitalization, the town is looking to improve zoning standards for creative property reuse and site design, introducing flexible strategies like floating zones or density bonuses to make non-conforming, vacant, or blighted lots more attractive to developers.

quotes.briefing_quote: According to census analysis, Grantsville's demographic character is rapidly shifting, marked by a median age that rose from 37 years in 2000 to 52 years in 2020. This change is driven by a 25% increase in the senior citizen population alongside declines in younger age cohorts.

Grantsville's historic built environment is legacy-rich but faces infrastructure challenges, including retaining parts of its original 1933 sanitary sewer system constructed with terra cotta pipes and brick manholes, which currently suffer from significant wet-weather infiltration and inflow.

A series of significant housing additions are altering the town's landscape, led by the North Hill Community, an active-adult residential development under construction with 50 single-family detached homes in its initial phase, and a planned 61-unit mixed-density project on Springs Road.

Given that over 60% of local housing units are rented and more than half of renters are housing cost-burdened, local planners recommend evaluating the zoning ordinance to reduce dimensional lot requirements and increase densities to foster more affordable, lower-maintenance workforce housing.

The town relies on proven local templates for affordable housing delivery, prominently citing Cassel Ridge East, a 36-unit multi-family affordable housing tax credit development completed in 2004 by the Garrett County Community Action Committee, as a template for low- to moderate-income housing.

quotes.briefing_quote: Described as a small, family-focused community with a primarily residential base, Loch Lynn Heights' layout features a commercial district situated along an active rail line, anchored by a highly active municipal recreational complex and wetland trail.

According to historical summaries, Loch Lynn Heights originally evolved from a Confederate major's farm into a thriving late 19th-century resort town powered by the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad, but declined as a resort during the early 1900s with the rise of automobile travel, followed later by a short-lived natural gas drilling boom in the 1950s.

Transportation planners highlight the Maryland Route 135 Pedestrian and Bicycle Concept Plan, a state-funded initiative designed to connect Loch Lynn Heights, Mountain Lake Park, and Oakland along a 1.5-mile corridor, introducing dedicated bike lanes and sidewalks to slow down fast-moving highway traffic.

The plan highlights the abandoned Mustang Property—a former moving and storage facility at the entrance of town—as a prime target for revitalization, noting that while it requires extensive work, it represents multiple redevelopment opportunities that could be integrated into a county-wide brownfields cleanup inventory.

Following the closure of the long-standing Loch Lynn Restaurant, the plan urges local leaders and developers to focus on appropriate commercial re-use of this prime entrance site, identifying a new restaurant, convenience store, or other neighborhood-serving businesses as ideal fits.

quotes.briefing_quote: The community of Hancock is experiencing notable demographic shifts, characterized by an aging population where approximately half of the residents are aged sixty or older. Adult children are largely leaving the town, resulting in smaller household sizes, while the local median income of approximately $38,000 remains about half that of the state average, reflecting its status as an economically depressed area.

Following the decline of the orchard industry in the 1980s and the closure of major factories in the 1990s and early 2000s, Hancock lost nearly 650 jobs, forcing workers to commute long distances and compelling the town to reinvent itself as a regional tourism, recreation, and light industrial hub.

The town is targeting the acquisition of 528 East Main Street to serve as a Career Training and Business Incubation Center to jump-start small local businesses and provide critical workforce development training in high-technology, IT, and healthcare fields.

The Western Maryland Rail Trail parking lot at Church and Main Streets represents the largest publicly owned downtown site, creating a substantial 'hole' in the continuous street façade; local planners suggest soliciting mixed-use development proposals that incorporate a covered public parking deck with upper floors of retail and housing.

As a successful precedent for adaptive reuse and historic preservation, the reconstructed Monterey House was transformed into a 25-unit senior housing project in the Town Center, addressing the housing needs of the area's growing elderly population.

quotes.briefing_quote: La Plata has successfully rebuilt after several natural disasters, including a devastating 2002 tornado, and has steadily evolved into a resilient bedroom community of just under 9,500 residents serving the metropolitan Washington, D.C., region and nearby military installations.

Originally founded in 1873 as a train stop along the Baltimore and Potomac Railroad, La Plata became the Charles County seat in 1892 after a fire destroyed the Port Tobacco courthouse, later experiencing significant highway-oriented growth following the 1940 opening of the Potomac River Bridge.

To better integrate anchor institutions into the community, local planners recommend establishing a Community and Campus Zone for Hospitals and Health Care Facilities that will consolidate parking requirements and encourage active, pedestrian-friendly street frontages near the medical center.

Urban design assessments suggest that the town should create developments with more density to differentiate the historic downtown core from surrounding low-density residential neighborhoods, while shifting retail storefront orientations toward active street frontages rather than rear parking lots.

Planners emphasize the importance of diversifying the town's single-family-dominated housing stock by promoting accessory dwelling units and mixed-use developments, which will provide viable housing options for young professionals and allow seniors to age in place.

quotes.briefing_quote: The plan highlights that Sharptown functions as a close-knit, family-oriented 'bedroom' community with several active stakeholder groups—including the historical commission, volunteer fire department, Lions Club, and American Legion—and local churches that help define the community's rural fabric.

The Town has focused its redevelopment efforts on the former Sharptown Elementary School, securing state grants to acquire the property and perform engineering studies to rehabilitate the blighted former school into a productive multi-purpose community center.

Despite a historic shipbuilding and industrial heritage, Sharptown’s commercial sector experienced a sharp decline after a 1953 fire destroyed the Marvel Package Company and the subsequent closure of the Bloch and Guggenheimer Pickle Factory in 2011.

As a successful precedent for blight elimination, the town used state funding to acquire and clean up a blighted parcel on Nanticoke Street, and subsequently donated the lot to Operation We Care for the construction of a single-family home for a local veteran.

For developers eyeing future construction, infrastructure capacity is a key constraint; the town suffers from severe inflow and infiltration issues within its wastewater collection system, meaning the town must correct sewer main infiltration before large-scale new developments can be accommodated.

Housing data reveals that 82.7% of the town's housing stock is owner-occupied, representing a highly stable residential base, though local planners note an increasing need for diverse options like senior-restricted subdivisions and 55-and-older developments to support the aging population.

quotes.briefing_quote: Crisfield remains a proud historical waterman community with a working waterfront culture and unique architectural style, where small mom-and-pop style businesses contribute to a distinct, close-knit local character despite facing geographic isolation and economic challenges.

The city has suffered long-term population decline, with the population decreasing by 28 percent between 1960 and 2020, which has left a legacy of vacant structures, housing blight, and underutilized commercial storefronts in the central business district.

The ongoing rehabilitation and adaptive reuse of the former Crisfield Armory, supported by $1 million in State Revitalization Grants, aims to eliminate a blighted landmark and establish a vital multi-purpose community facility for indoor sports, youth activities, and public events.

Developers must navigate severe environmental constraints, as almost the entire city is situated in a 100-year floodplain where historic downtown buildings are highly susceptible to chronic flooding and cannot be easily flood-proofed due to strict historic preservation guidelines.

The success of the Crisfield Business Development and Façade Improvement Program, which distributed $143,330 in grants since 2019, demonstrates how targeting exterior renovations can successfully leverage private investments to remove blight and stabilize commercial corridors.

quotes.briefing_quote: Almost all housing in Johnston Square is currently affordable by regional definitions, as only roughly 4% of households need to pay more than $1,500 per month in housing costs. However, much of this housing is 'naturally occurring' affordable housing and therefore not protected from escalating rents or property taxes, nor does much of it prevent its residents from facing housing cost burdens.

Following a similar pattern of dedicating urban squares to improve the value of new homes, the Vickers family sold land to the City for the purpose of creating Johnston Square Park. During the second half of the 20th Century, Johnston Square became a victim to discriminatory lending practices which resulted in disinvestment, concentrated poverty, population loss and abandonment.

In 2019, the Partners worked with Baltimore City to secure site control over all abandoned and City-owned properties in Johnston Square. During the ten-year term of a Land Disposition Agreement, Baltimore City will acquire and convey vacant properties to the Partners to redevelop vacant parcels and to renovate or newly construct scores of houses in order to rebuild a healthy, viable and equitable residential market.

Based on current market data, homebuyer demand in Johnston Square will not support sales prices sufficient to cover the cost to renovate abandoned homes (more than $250,000). Subsidizing the sale of the renovated homes in the first years of redevelopment—as was done in Greenmount West and Oliver—will help restore the market to a condition where home prices can equal the cost of renovation.

The catalyst for the market improvements in Greenmount West and Oliver between 2011 and 2017 are instructive for Johnston Square. Both neighborhoods benefited from focused redevelopment efforts that eliminated blight and reoccupied vacant property. By using subsidy to support for-sale and rental production, homes in these areas could be redeveloped and sold or leased at levels higher than existing market prices, but lower than their development costs.

quotes.briefing_quote: To address the needs of an aging population, town planners aim to increase housing opportunities for the senior and aging community by utilizing town-owned property along Carpenter's Point Road for a potential senior housing development and adjacent community center.

Reflecting on its coastal legacy, the plan highlights Charlestown's historical significance as the first major 18th-century seaport on the Upper Chesapeake Bay, boasting many preserved 18th-century homes, historic taverns, and a waterfront rich in historic and recreational assets.

To address auto-pedestrian safety, local officials plan to integrate traffic calming and green stormwater infrastructure at Bladen and Market Streets, introducing a new traffic circle and safer walking routes to the local elementary school.

quotes.briefing_quote: Based on current market data, homebuyer demand in Johnston Square will not support sales prices sufficient to cover the cost to renovate abandoned homes (more than $250,000). Subsidizing the sale of the renovated homes in the first years of redevelopment—as was done in Greenmount West and Oliver—will help restore the market to a condition where home prices can equal the cost of renovation.

The catalyst for the market improvements in Greenmount West and Oliver between 2011 and 2017 are instructive for Johnston Square. Both neighborhoods benefited from focused redevelopment efforts that eliminated blight and reoccupied vacant property. By using subsidy to support for-sale and rental production, homes in these areas could be redeveloped and sold or leased at levels higher than existing market prices, but lower than their development costs.

quotes.briefing_quote: Oliver is a historic neighborhood characterized by primarily single-family rowhouse development and vast open spaces, with excellent transit access to downtown and nearby job hubs.

The neighborhood's historic housing stock varies by street hierarchy: builders constructed three-bay-wide houses on main north-south arteries, narrower two-bay houses on connecting east-west streets, and tiny, two-story Italianate 'alley' houses on mid-block streets like Bethel, Dallas, and Spring to provide affordable options.

To balance local housing options and boost homeownership toward the citywide average, the plan advises developers to target 80% to 85% market-rate units for new multifamily projects along major corridors.

Plan contributors emphasize that new single-family infill should not exceed three stories and should voluntarily align with the Commission for Historical and Architectural Preservation (CHAP) design guidelines to protect Oliver's historic architecture.

The National Great Blacks in Wax Museum is advancing a multi-phase, 40,000-square-foot expansion plan along East North Avenue, which will feature a new museum center, children's spaces, a theater, and a public outdoor sculpture garden.

The 2022 completion of Sojourner Place, a 70-unit affordable housing development with ground-floor community amenities, serves as a successful precedent for modern residential infill on Harford Avenue.

The proposed Hoffman Greenway connects the Oliver Community Farm to neighboring Johnston Square's green corridor initiatives, utilizing a shared infrastructure path above the Northeast Corridor rail line.

quotes.briefing_quote: Smithsburg presents a close-knit community of 2,974 residents with a median household income of $69,474. The population is primarily a bedroom community for commuters working in larger metropolitan areas like Baltimore and Washington, D.C., and features a highly educated populace with over 93% of adults holding at least a high school diploma.

The town recently approved a Master Development Plan for multigenerational communities, emphasizing open space and stormwater quality, though its physical integration with the historic Town Center is currently restricted by surrounding county lands.

Planning coordinators noted that local commercial property owners in the Town Center often lack the capital necessary to rehabilitate historic properties, while the town's small tax revenues are primarily absorbed by basic property maintenance.

To preserve neighborhood character, local stakeholders recommend establishing license and inspection requirements for all rental properties and aggressively addressing maintenance code violations, particularly near the historic Town Center where absentee landlord issues persist.

Smithsburg retains a vibrant small-town atmosphere and rural setting, bolstered by highly supported local public schools, an active monthly Farmers' Market (noted as the best attended in Washington County in 2021), and close proximity to the Appalachian Trail.

quotes.briefing_quote: To help residential and commercial property owners maintain and restore their buildings, the town established a popular Facade Improvement Grant opportunity through the newly designated Main Street Williamsport program, creating a waiting list due to high demand.

The completion of the new National Park Service Headquarters within town limits, along with ongoing renovations of other historic properties on the grounds, is expected to significantly increase foot traffic and bring new jobs to the community.

A private development group, Port44 LLC, has acquired and is rehabilitating several blighted buildings along Conococheague Street, helping to attract new businesses to the downtown area including eateries and a bicycle shop.
Heavy truck traffic routed through the downtown area creates persistent congestion, an issue exacerbated by ongoing regional construction and frequent backups on Interstate 81.
Central Williamsport features shallow bedrock and extremely rocky silty clay loam soils, which present a unique physical obstacle to new excavation and structural development.

With over 50% of the population consisting of seniors or youth, the town faces an aging housing stock where both home interiors and exteriors require updates to support elderly and retiree residents aging in place.

Williamsport faces severe physical constraints to housing expansion because the town has no room to grow for more housing to be established or built within its current municipal boundaries, driving interest in potential annexation.

quotes.briefing_quote: The City Center's role as the region's economic and cultural hub was heavily reinforced by the completion of the Urban Improvement Project. This major public-private effort included the expansion of the Maryland Theatre in 2019, the Barbara Ingram School for the Arts expansion in 2020, and the completion of the Hagerstown Cultural Trail, which has successfully boosted investor and lender confidence downtown.

To demonstrate the viability of downtown residential markets, the City and the University System of Maryland at Hagerstown partnered with private developers on student housing demonstration projects, including Patterson Hall, 140 W. Antietam Street, and the conversion of the historic Hamilton Hotel into 37 units targeting students and young professionals.

While demand for new construction Class A office space remains weak, the City's economic incentive programs have successfully facilitated historic downtown office renovations, including the Professional Arts Building, Mulberry Lofts, Wareham Building, and the Masonic Temple.

Plans are underway for the construction of the new Hagerstown Multi-use Sports and Events Facility, which is anticipated to be completed in 2023 alongside a new municipal parking deck scheduled for construction in FY 2023-FY 2024.
The Sustainable Community Area contains the historic urban core of Hagerstown, which continues to experience challenges for redevelopment and remains the City’s top priority area for revitalization.

quotes.briefing_quote: The core of Ellicott City contains the Ellicott City Historic District, which is highly vulnerable to the risk of flooding as it sits at the confluence of three major tributaries: the Hudson, Tiber, and New Cut Branches.

Planning staff noted that steep elevations and a lack of available land for greenfield development severely limit infill housing opportunities in Ellicott City, making housing affordability an ongoing challenge.

The Thomas Isaac Log Cabin, built around 1780 and relocated after the 2018 flood, stands as a symbol of early European colonial development and 19th-century African American heritage in the Patapsco River Valley.

The Burgess Mill Station II project serves as a key precedent, delivering 53 mixed-income rental apartments utilizing sustainable environmental design standards, including micro-bioretention facilities that exceed county regulatory requirements.

County officials highlighted the acquisition of a $75 million loan to fund the Extended North Tunnel project, a massive flood mitigation initiative designed to divert 26,000 gallons of water per second away from Ellicott City's commercial core.

To stimulate local economic revitalization, the Department of Public Works has petitioned to rezone the historic, now-vacant Courthouse from Historic Office to Historic Commercial, opening up opportunities for creative adaptive reuse.

Developers should be aware that flood zone designations prohibit the use of federal Community Development Block Grant or HOME funds for new construction or redevelopment projects in Ellicott City, restricting funding support to low-income resident assistance.

A major addition to the local green space network is nearly complete at Bollinger Park, which will introduce 102 acres of walking trails, pollinator gardens, and open space to the community.

In a highly competitive, post-pandemic real estate market, developers are not voluntarily providing senior-restricted housing units because covenants decrease a property's immediate sales potential, leaving the city without the financial leverage to incentivize senior-dedicated infill.

The concentration of rental housing within the historic core makes it ideal for targeted housing reinvestment and rehabilitation funding, though tight supply has historically allowed landlords to defer property maintenance without risking vacancies.

quotes.briefing_quote: Historians and planners trace the town's evolution back over two centuries, noting that Millington grew up as a small village on the Chester River, originating from a late 17th-century ferry crossing and a 1754 land grant secured near a key river crossing.

Planning commissioners emphasized that while maintaining the Town Center as a viable commercial area will be a challenge due to limited vacant land, any proposed infill and redevelopment should be done to reflect the existing land development pattern and the architectural character of its surroundings, ensuring new buildings front the street with parking at the rear.

A series of tragic fires in 1818, 1879, and 1904 destroyed large swaths of the town, but between 1905 and 1920, Millington was rebuilt using more modern construction methods and architectural practices, which created the cohesive historic district we see today.

To accommodate new residents, the Town designated the newly annexed Freeman Evans Farm as a Planned Neighborhood Development with the goal of creating a mixed-use development that incorporates a variety of housing options, different population densities, nonresidential establishments, green spaces, and recreational facilities.

The historic Bailey Hotel at the crossroads of Cypress and Sassafras Streets represents a key local design precedent, notable because it combines a mansard roof, typical of the French Second Empire Style, with common Victorian elements, showing how late-period architectural styles successfully integrated into the town.

A comparative housing analysis reveals that while home values in Millington are lower than in nearby areas like Chestertown or Galena, its median contract rent remains disproportionately high, indicating that the apparent lack of available rental housing may be driving up the cost of rental housing across these small Eastern Shore municipalities.

quotes.briefing_quote: Community members emphasize that the highest planning priority is the care and protection of its greatest attribute: the small-town character of Galena. This scale is defined by easy walking distances, porches, sidewalks, and safe streets that connect its diverse mixture of ages, incomes, and architectural styles.

Galena's history can be traced back over 250 years to 1763 when the settlement was called Downes Tavern, serving as a stop on the historic route between Rock Hall and Philadelphia. Over the centuries, the town developed as a vital farm service community at the junction of two major roads, built on deep, well-drained soils that still support the lush canopy of trees and flowers defining its physical identity.

The municipal wastewater system was modernized with Enhanced Nutrient Removal technology and reserves 30,000 gallons per day to serve developed portions of the Georgetown area. This was initiated to address a public health emergency caused by failing septic systems on lots too small to support on-site replacements.

To ensure new development fits seamlessly, community guidelines are strongly opposed to formulaic building designs, franchise architecture, and generic signage that impair the town's aesthetic. New construction must prioritize traditional building practices, utilizing residential styles along Main and Cross Streets as the design model.

While single-family homes and duplexes are easily accommodated, current zoning restricts denser layouts. The plan suggests the town should consider adopting zoning standards for accessory dwelling units and smaller-scale multi-family types like triplexes and quadplexes to expand missing-middle workforce housing options without disrupting neighborhood character.

The town's development guidelines emphasize that any future growth must respect the predominant residential character of Galena along with its historic housing styles, pedestrian-friendly walking scale, and strong history of homeownership.

quotes.briefing_quote: Denton will be an innovative, healthy, safe, well-balanced community that protects its historical integrity, preserves its unique natural resources, enhances its economic vitality, and maintains its unique small-town character.

The Harriet Tubman Underground Railroad Byway traces the likely movements of freedom seekers across the landscape, connecting several historic towns, including Preston, Denton, Hillsboro, and Greensboro, which risked everything to secure freedom for themselves and others.

A Preliminary Engineering Report commissioned by Caroline County will examine alternative methods of providing sewer service to West Denton, which will be included in Denton's Annexation Plan if the costs of providing sewer service are supportable.

Flexible development standards and processes for infill and redevelopment proposals should apply in the old town Denton neighborhoods. These are areas of the Town where most lots are nonconforming in some respect, and projects deemed context-appropriate should be provided with a path forward.

The Heritage Center for Caroline County is an example of a capital project in Denton's Targeted Investment Zone (TIZ) that is eligible for funding under Maryland's Heritage Areas Management Program, which will renovate the former Town Hall to enhance heritage tourism.

quotes.briefing_quote: Prospective restaurateurs in Denton face administrative hurdles, as national chains and local establishments wishing to serve alcohol are hindered by a Caroline County law requiring the bar owner or manager to reside within the county to obtain a liquor license.

A developer is driving significant downtown commercial revitalization with a $2-million-dollar renovation of 322 Market Street, creating capacity for up to 20 new businesses and supporting an active, pedestrian-friendly downtown environment.

Housing options in Denton are expanding with workforce-oriented projects, including the 63-unit Gardens development and the proposed 44-townhome Denton LLC community on Camp Road, designed to provide high-quality, energy-efficient housing for local professionals such as teachers and firefighters.

While high-speed broadband is readily available within Denton's town limits, surrounding rural areas suffer from inconsistent coverage, presenting an opportunity for a developer to fund and install high-speed fiber infrastructure throughout the broader county footprint.

Commercial growth is accelerating along the Route 404 corridor with the groundbreaking of Denton Plaza II, which has already attracted prominent national and regional tenants including Aldi, Popeyes, and Dairy Queen.

quotes.briefing_quote: The Hampstead Historic District contains 226 properties within a 98-acre boundary recognized by the Maryland Inventory of Historic Properties, reflecting the town's pride in maintaining its distinctive small-town charm and friendly, family-oriented atmosphere.

In 2015, the Florida Rock property on Houcksville Road was zoned Restricted Industrial. Due to infrastructure costs, the owners successfully rezoned the 117-acre property to R-7,500 Residential. The property, now known as Hampstead Overlook, is planned to be developed as a Planned Unit Development of 255 homes, providing a mix of single-family homes and townhomes.

To reduce storefront vacancies and diversify the business base, the town seeks to create a mixed-use overlay zone in the downtown district. This would allow a mixture of residential and commercial use within the same structure, making properties more desirable and encouraging interior rehabilitation.

Growth in the downtown district faces challenges as historic core building footprints are not attractive to regional and national chains, and street parking remains a constraint with only two public off-street parking lots currently available.

In 2016, Northside Estates received approval to build a 17-home community off Main Street, just north of Route 482. Fifteen homes have been constructed and sold, and the final two homes are scheduled for completion in 2021.

quotes.briefing_quote: Hampstead is envisioned as the quintessential American small town, offering a clean, safe, and attractive environment with quiet, well-maintained residential neighborhoods that are highly desirable for families.
Local planners emphasize that the era of large-scale residential growth is largely over, prompting a strategic focus on infill development, water resource balance, and commercial revitalization.
The historic routing of the railroad in 1879 served as the defining catalyst for modern growth, boosting local agricultural profitability and driving a horizontal expansion of the town grid.
The long-awaited opening of the Hampstead Bypass has diverted heavy through-traffic from the historic downtown core, presenting a unique opportunity for Main Street revitalization.
The successful conversion of the historic Hampstead School into 84 units of affordable senior housing stands as an outstanding local precedent for high-quality adaptive reuse.

To protect municipal character, town and county officials are collaborating to establish a permanent greenbelt between the corporate limits of Hampstead and Manchester, ensuring the towns do not merge.

Union Bridge's rich historic identity is anchored by its National Register Historic District status, the Heart of the Civil War Heritage Area designation, and landmarks such as the Western Maryland Railroad Museum.

quotes.briefing_quote: The Town of Barclay is a small family community in northern Queen Anne's County at the crossroads of MD 313 and MD 302, comprised mostly of single-family homes and has a diverse and multi-generational population.

Barclay's size has grown little over the last several decades, due in part to natural soil limitations and the lack of public water and wastewater facilities. The potential exists for the Town to grow in size if water and public sewer are made available.
The community that was to become Sudlersville took root in 1740 when Joseph Sudler purchased 800 acres. After the Civil War, the railroad laid track to the town, bringing a period of growth.

The Town has adequate land capacity within its corporate limits to accommodate expected growth over the next few decades, and Sudlersville anticipates annexation of Inner-Loop properties as water and sewer become available.

Town planners noted that Sudlersville residents are connected to a water system with treatment designed to reduce arsenic, which was established alongside a 500,000-gallon elevated storage tank and expanded water mains to ensure safe drinking water access.

Planning documents note that residents in Barclay historically obtained water from shallow private wells, but increasing nitrate and nitrogen levels in the shallow aquifer have forced new and replacement wells to be drilled deeper into the Aquia aquifer.

quotes.briefing_quote: To address barriers to smart growth and encourage revitalization, the Town of Sudlersville updated its zoning ordinance to allow for floating zones, Planned Neighborhood Development, and mixed-use development in the Town Center district, permitting commercial space on the first floor and residential units on the second.

Sudlersville's zoning structure encourages redevelopment and compatible infill by designating Town Central Commercial and Town Residential districts, which are specifically designed to preserve the historical core and minimize nonconforming uses.

Sudlersville is currently upgrading its wastewater treatment plant to include Biological Nutrient Removal/Enhanced Nutrient Removal and is extending public water and sewer lines to the neighboring town of Barclay to help address issues with failing septic systems.

While the town lacks specialized housing for low-income and disabled populations, the immediate local priority is to provide dedicated senior housing to support Sudlersville's growing elderly population and allow them to remain in the community.
Sudlersville offers an affordable housing market with costs below the national average, characterized by a median rent of $522 and an average single-family home value of approximately $173,228.

Plans are underway to revitalize a previously abandoned old school building into a new community center, which is envisioned to house a community space, office facilities, and potential veteran apartments.

quotes.briefing_quote: Demographic trends show that Centreville's recent slower pace of household formation has led to a shifting age profile, indicating an overall 20-year trend toward an older population, with those under 18 now comprising only 22.9 percent of the town's residents.

Historically, the town's share of the county's population fell from a high of 12.4 percent in 1950 to a low of 4.9 percent in 2000, which was primarily the result of the build-out of Kent Island combined with essentially no growth in Centreville itself.

To facilitate planned growth and address future needs, the Town is preparing to expand and modernize its wastewater treatment plant capacity from 542,000 gallons per day to 1.0 million or 1.25 million gallons per day, alongside establishing new effluent disposal measures.

The plan outlines a major transportation expansion, highlighting the creation of the East Side Major Collector, which will extend from Wexford Drive to Taylor Mill Road to distribute traffic and provide congestion relief to the busy Route 213 corridor.

When evaluating new developments, the Town aims to prioritize allocations for proposals that support a 'complete neighborhoods' approach, featuring intergenerational housing, cluster designs to maximize open spaces, and highly energy-efficient utility delivery.

The plan highlights The Willows at Centreville on Little Hut Drive as a successful precedent of a mixed-income residential community, offering 70 units of both market-rate and low-income options built under the Federal Low Income Housing Tax Credit program.

quotes.briefing_quote: A major zoning and development challenge arose when the volunteer fire company proposed redeveloping its station in the historic town center. Local leaders invested significant time and resources to alter the course of that redevelopment so that it would fit compatibly into the historic district, successfully preserving the downtown character.

The Town successfully preserved a highly visible historic asset by updating and furnishing the old Queenstown Bank Building at 406 Main Street to serve as the new Town Hall and community gathering space, which now accommodates five times the capacity of the previous meeting facility.

quotes.briefing_quote: Based on current market data, homebuyer demand in Johnston Square will not support sales prices sufficient to cover the cost to renovate abandoned homes (more than $250,000). Subsidizing the sale of the renovated homes in the first years of redevelopment—as was done in Greenmount West and Oliver—will help restore the market to a condition where home prices can equal the cost of renovation.

The catalyst for the market improvements in Greenmount West and Oliver between 2011 and 2017 are instructive for Johnston Square. Both neighborhoods benefited from focused redevelopment efforts that eliminated blight and reoccupied vacant property. By using subsidy to support for-sale and rental production, homes in these areas could be redeveloped and sold or leased at levels higher than existing market prices, but lower than their development costs.

quotes.briefing_quote: Essex remains a historically resilient community with a diverse and stable population, though recent data highlights a slight increase in the median age to 41.1 years alongside a growing Hispanic and Latino population that now comprises over 7 percent of the local fabric.

A significant challenge for future development is the lack of modern infrastructure, with only 9.5 percent of the Essex Sustainable Community area currently draining to stormwater management facilities that provide water quality benefits, especially along the Eastern Boulevard commercial corridor.

County planners emphasize the need to encourage reinvestment and modernization in older shopping centers such as Middlesex Shopping Center and Hawthorne Plaza, aligning these sites with updated commercial policies and potential mixed-use zoning.

To stimulate local economic activity, the plan recommends revising zoning in the commercial core to allow for increased density and mixed-use developments, including workforce housing above retail along the Eastern Boulevard corridor.

The Cal Ripken, Sr. Foundation Youth Development Park represents a highly successful model of public-private collaboration, leveraging county, State, and foundation resources to replace aging infrastructure with state-of-the-art synthetic turf and LED lighting.

The community-led installation of the Essex Gateway Landmark Sculpture over the Back River bridge stands as a powerful symbol of local pride and renewal, celebrating the area's rich maritime, industrial, and diverse cultural history.

With 45 percent of local housing units being renter-occupied, stakeholders noted that neighborhoods are feeling increasingly transient, prompting calls for expanded homeownership counseling and targeted outreach to first-time homebuyers.

quotes.briefing_quote: Between 2018 and 2022, Reisterstown experienced demographic stability and growth, with the average median household income rising to $105,000, higher homeownership rates, and a slight aging of the population.

The acquisition of the 3.79-acre Woodley Avenue Park site in November 2022 provides a critical opportunity to expand open space and connect the historic Main Street with the nearby Franklin Woodland Trails network.

Developers and planners face challenges such as zoning constraints and community opposition to higher-density projects in Reisterstown, where low-density residential zoning surrounds a commercial corridor that could otherwise support mixed-use infill.

Since 2020, the Reisterstown Improvement Association's Facade Improvement Grant Program has successfully enhanced 14 commercial facades, demonstrating the viability of small-scale aesthetic improvements to support local business retention.

To establish a cohesive aesthetic, local partners commissioned the Reisterstown Main Street Streetscape Design Recommendations, aiming to eventually adopt these guidelines formally within the county's development review process.

quotes.briefing_quote: The Town of Trappe is a residential community with a mix of older but fairly well-maintained housing stock, surrounded by working agriculture with little to no commercial or industrial base.

The town center at the crossroads of Maple and Main Streets was thriving in the 1950s and 1960s when the main highway ran through the center of town, but has since struggled to retain small businesses.
A major planned development on the east side of Route 50 has yet to be built, leaving 2,501 planned residential units on hold due to economic shifts and county impact fees.

quotes.briefing_quote: Socio-economic and housing data show that Trappe is a community primarily composed of working-class households and families, where residents are more likely to rent and have lower average incomes than those in the rest of Talbot County.
Sometime during the Revolutionary years, the name 'the Trap' began to appear in land records to refer to this crossroads hamlet, sparking numerous colorful local legends about its origin.

To accommodate working-class residents, local guidance advises balancing allowable residential densities with development design standards to keep housing costs as low as possible without sacrificing neighborhood quality.

While the Town has identified areas along US 50 suitable for Highway Commercial Mixed-Use development, water and sewer services must be extended at the developer's expense before any new construction can proceed.

Growth projections show that the initial phase of the Lakeside project is expected to deliver approximately 320 dwelling units, serving as a major driver of residential expansion in the planning area.

quotes.briefing_quote: Oxford has seen very little change in its demographic makeup over the years, remaining a small retirement community where age, race, household size, and income experience minimal variation over time.

The town successfully acquired and stabilized the Historic Oxford Mews, a dilapidated commercial anchor in the historic district, and is actively seeking proposals for its final redevelopment as a mixed-use commercial building.

While many property owners maintain their properties well, Oxford's aging population on fixed budgets faces significant challenges keeping up with the expensive exterior maintenance required for large historic homes.

Characterized by its historic brick sidewalks and narrow, pedestrian-friendly streets, Oxford remains a completely walkable and bikeable community where vehicular travel is largely unnecessary for daily movement.

Operating since 1683, the Oxford-Bellevue Ferry is a critical cultural asset, but because it is a privately owned amenity, finding financial assistance to offset high annual maintenance costs is essential to ensure its continuous operation.

Built in 1770, the Barnaby House stands as the oldest private residence in Oxford on its original foundation, and local advocates are exploring public-private ventures to prevent the structural decline of this vacant historic landmark.

quotes.briefing_quote: According to National Register of Historic Places documentation, the community is defined by its pristine rural setting, narrow, curving streets, and great trees, alongside an exceptionally intact collection of unaltered late-18th to early-20th century Federal and Victorian architecture.

Founded in 1794 by Quaker settler Richard Thomas, Brookeville holds a unique place in national history as the 'Capital for a Day' where President James Madison sought refuge and conducted the business of the United States government in 1814 after the British invasion of Washington.

With the imminent completion of the Brookeville Bypass, the town is poised to reclaim High Street and West Market Street from heavy regional arterial traffic, diverting over 10,000 vehicles per day and allowing these corridors to function as quiet, walkable local streets.

To protect the town's historic rural aesthetic, the Historic Village Residential (HVR) zone permits single-family homes at a base density of one unit per acre but strongly encourages the clustering of new development on smaller lots to preserve remaining acreage as private or public open space.

The Powers' Woods subdivision at the end of North Street serves as a precedent for modern in-fill development, where a three-lot residential subdivision successfully integrated an existing house with new construction and dedicated adjoining land to the town to establish Powers' Wood Park.

quotes.briefing_quote: Historically, the Town of Indian Head was originally part of Chapman's Landing in 1654, later transitioning into a residential hub in the 1890s as workers migrated to support the newly established Naval Proving Ground, which remains the county's largest employer today.

Indian Head is described as a serene and picturesque waterfront community that maintains a warm, small-town atmosphere while supporting a diverse, highly skilled population and active cultural hubs like the Black Box Theatre.

To foster more vibrant and viable commercial enterprises, local planners recommend revising mixed-use regulations to encourage both residential and commercial uses on the same parcel, rather than permitting developers to build one to the exclusion of the other.

While infill development is highly encouraged to leverage existing infrastructure, developers face site constraints like poor soils and wetlands, alongside community concerns regarding insufficient parking in the older parts of town and limited sewer and water tap allocations.

A major anchor project is underway along the Route 210 corridor, where the College of Southern Maryland's Velocity Center is being established at Velocity Park to serve as a hub for professional development, entrepreneurship, and community collaboration.

The Riverwatch development and the Villages of Potomac represent successful local precedents where higher-density, multi-family housing projects were successfully built along the Route 210 mixed-use corridor, proving the viability of compact, walkable designs.

quotes.briefing_quote: Town leaders focused their Sustainable Community boundary on the entire municipality, with a particular emphasis on the Route 210 corridor. They noted that this highway corridor serves as the gateway to the community, but has unfortunately fallen into a neglected condition.

Although there is a stable base of single-family homes and affordable rental options, much of the housing stock in Indian Head is aging and poorly maintained in certain locations, prompting local officials to recommend rehabilitation grants and low-interest loans to address property maintenance.

To stimulate commercial redevelopment along the main corridor, the Town expanded the Mixed-Use zone along the entirety of Route 210, demolished several dilapidated buildings, and waived permitting fees for commercial properties to attract investment.

A major public space project, the construction of the Boardwalk and Living Shoreline, commenced in late 2020 to offer expanded outdoor recreation options for residents and act as a regional draw for visitors.

quotes.briefing_quote: The boundary of the sustainable community area includes key commercial areas, business parks, and older residential neighborhoods such as Saint Charles and Pinefield, emphasizing a balanced approach to both transit-oriented commercial redevelopment and neighborhood preservation.

For developers looking at the Waldorf Urban Redevelopment Corridor, the county notes that progress has been historically hindered by inadequate sewer infrastructure, drainage issues, and highly fractured, narrowly shaped lots that make consolidation necessary for mixed-use success.

As part of transitional zoning strategies, county planners are drafting provisions to increase regulatory flexibility for existing businesses and developed properties in the urban corridor until major mixed-use redevelopment starts transforming the area.

Significant economic momentum is building in the area, highlighted by the reactivation of a long-vacant 200,000-square-foot warehouse as an Amazon Last Mile Delivery facility, alongside massive new healthcare investments from MedStar Shah and Kaiser Permanente.

Residents will benefit from the construction of the new 216-acre Waldorf Park, which is designed to meet active and passive recreational needs with lighted sports fields, an adaptive special-needs playground, and fitness trails.
